axes.model_access:
**Can do: multi-model + BYOK, officially stated as "pick a model per conversation".**

**Official wording**: "Pick a model per conversation, bring your own provider API keys, and track credit usage"

The model sources of the Build tier on the pricing page are:

**Official wording**: "frontier and open-source models from OpenAI, Anthropic, z.ai, and more"

**BYOK has tier boundaries.**

The official pricing table marks **"Bring your own API key"** and **"Custom inference endpoint"** as:

**Official wording**: "Individuals and orgs up to 10 people"

That is, individuals and orgs up to 10 people can use it.

The Enterprise tier additionally has **BYOLLM**:

**Official wording**: "Route inference through your own cloud (BYOLLM)"

(meaning: inference goes through your own cloud.)

**Switching models**: on the CLI side you can pick a model per session.
Execution profiles can also set a `base_model` override.

**Not verified: the official pricing page does not list the full model catalog**
(pricing and agents/cli pages checked.)
axes.runtime:
**Can do: the same agent has three run surfaces, CLI-first.**

Official docs wording:

**Official wording**: "Warp is an open-source Agentic Development Environment"

Three entry points share one **Warp Agent**:

**Official wording**: "In the Warp app"

**Official wording**: "In any terminal, with the Warp Agent CLI"

**Official wording**: "In the cloud, as a cloud agent"

**The CLI is a standalone terminal program.**

**Official wording**: "a standalone terminal program that runs the Warp Agent"

It is itself:

**Official wording**: "a native terminal multiplexer"

It ships its own PTY, so it runs inside any terminal emulator, **including over SSH**.

The launch command is `warp` (the cloud side additionally has the `oz` command).

**Accounts, rules, skills and model access are consistent across the three entry points.**
The official docs note the CLI does not require installing the Warp desktop app.

This entry records the CLI form.
Differences vs the desktop app and the cloud agent follow the official pages.
axes.local_files:
**Can do: works inside a local checkout, changes presented as diffs.**

The "Project context" section of the official CLI page states the agent automatically reads project rules
(e.g. `AGENTS.md`), skills and MCP config.

File changes are presented as diffs.
By default `apply_code_diffs` is `agent_decides`.

**But file edits still prompt every time.**

**Official wording**: "you always review a diff before it's applied"

**Directory authorization**: execution profiles have `directory_allowlist`, controlling

**Official wording**: "Directories the agent may read without approval"

**Codebase indexing is capped per tier** (pricing page):

- Free 3 codebases / 3,000 files each
- Build and Max 40 / 100,000 files each
- Business 80
- Enterprise custom

**Not verified: the indexing algorithm and first-index time cost (not stated officially)**
(pricing and agents/cli pages checked.)
axes.background:
**Can do: the cloud background form is explicit; this is a true background surface.**

Terminal agents bind to the session.
But the official docs list **Automation Platform** and **cloud agents** separately:

**Official wording**: "Run background agent work in the cloud"

It can be triggered by triggers, schedules, integrations and the API.
Officially named uses include issue triage, pull request review, periodic maintenance.

**Warp Factories** goes further: a group of cloud agents attached to a repository.
It takes work from Slack / GitHub / Linear / Jira, runs triage → spec → implement → review,
and usually produces a PR.

The CLI side also has **cloud handoff**.
It can hand a session to a cloud agent, and pull a cloud run back into the terminal to continue.

**Cloud agent concurrency and compute are tiered** (pricing page):

- Free limited
- Build 20 concurrent / 2 vCPU 4 GiB
- Max 20 / 4 vCPU 8 GiB
- Business 80 / 8 vCPU 16 GiB
- Enterprise custom
axes.tools:
**Can do: in-terminal agent + complete MCP support (separate local and cloud stacks).**

Built-in capabilities center on the terminal:

- natural-language prompting
- **agent session transcripts** (streaming responses, Markdown, file diffs, tool calls, plans and task lists)
- running shell commands in the same input
- cloud handoff and multi-agent coordination

Warp Drive provides reusable objects: Workflows / Notebooks / Prompts / environment variables and more.

**MCP (local agent)**: officially supports

**Official wording**: "Streamable HTTP and SSE"

plus CLI (Command) local servers.

Config splits into project-level `.warp/.mcp.json` and global `~/.warp/.mcp.json`.
**It can also read third-party agents' MCP configs** (Claude Code, Codex etc.).
There is also the built-in skill `/agent-add-mcp`.
Auth supports env vars, OAuth one-click install and custom headers.
On security:

**Official wording**: "Project-scoped servers never auto-spawn"

**MCP (cloud agent)**: three reference styles supported.

- `command`/`args` (stdio)
- `url` (Streamable HTTP / SSE)
- `warp_id` (referencing an already-authorized hosted server)

OAuth goes through managed MCP installation.
axes.context:
**Can do: sessions persist to the account; exit-and-resume and switching are supported.**

Official CLI page wording:

**Official wording**: "Conversations save to your Warp account, so you can exit and resume later or switch between them"

On the interaction side `/status` shows the current session name and ID.

**Project context is auto-injected**: the agent automatically reads project rules (e.g. `AGENTS.md`),
skills and MCP servers.

Prompts saved in Warp Drive are available once logged in.

**But the official docs state only prompt-type objects work in the CLI.**

**Official wording**: "other Warp Drive object types aren't available in the CLI"

**Cross-agent memory** is listed under Enterprise as:

**Official wording**: "Cross-harness agent memory (Research Preview)"

**Not verified: context compaction strategy and cross-project memory boundaries (not stated officially)**
(agents/cli and warp-drive pages checked.)
axes.permissions:
**Can do: execution profile + three-tier values + auto-approve, an in-terminal approval model.**

Official wording:

**Official wording**: "Every action the agent proposes ... is checked against your active execution profile"

Permission values come in three tiers:

- **`agent_decides`** — proceeds on its own when confident, asks when unsure
- **`always_ask`** — asks every time
- **`always_allow`** — never asks

By default shell commands, file edits, file reads and MCP tool calls
are all `agent_decides`.
**File edits under `agent_decides` still prompt every time**, to guarantee:

**Official wording**: "always review a diff before it's applied"

There are also these items:

- `command_allowlist` / `command_denylist` (the denylist requires approval even under `always_allow`)
- `directory_allowlist`
- `write_to_pty`
- `run_agents`
- `ask_user_question`

**Auto-approve** (`/auto-approve` or `Ctrl+Shift+I`) grants full autonomy.
Its scope is a single session; new sessions default to off.
By default it bypasses the command denylist (can be turned off).
But denylists set by team admins in the Admin Panel are never bypassed.

Execution profiles are stored locally only, not synced to the cloud.
axes.fit:
**Fits: users who do both command execution and coding-agent work in the terminal, and want team collaboration and cloud automation.**

**Especially fits**:

- teams wanting to standardize terminal workflows into Workflows / Notebooks
- teams wanting to hand background work like issue triage / PR review to cloud agents
- enterprises needing SSO / data governance / self-hosted cloud agents

**Does not fit**:

- users who never touch terminal agents and just want a classic terminal

The Free tier can serve as a modern terminal.
But cloud agents, Warp Drive collaboration and codebase indexing all have quota ceilings.

sections.变更记录说明:
This object has its own changelog, and it is one of this site's rare **high-frequency releases**.

| Surface | Cadence | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| Product updates | usually every Thursday | `docs.warp.dev/changelog` (with per-year pages 2021–2026) |

**There is no single version number.**

Warp releases by "week" rather than by semver.
So when citing changes, write a date, not a version number.

This is the same kind of pitfall as Codex `rust-v*` and Crush `nightly`.
sections.三种入口，一个 agent:
The official docs explicitly place the same **Warp Agent** on three run surfaces:

```
In the Warp app · In any terminal (Warp Agent CLI) · In the cloud (cloud agent)
```

**This means quotas, account, rules and skills are one shared set.**

The CLI side additionally stresses it is **"a native terminal multiplexer"** — it ships its own PTY.
So it can share the same terminal with the agent to run interactive commands, **and it works over SSH**.

This is what separates a "terminal agent" from a "GUI terminal emulator".
sections.Warp Drive 是它的协作底座:
Warp Drive turns Workflows (parameterized commands), Notebooks (interactive runbooks),
Prompts and environment variables into **real-time-synced team objects**.

This is its organizational surface, unlike a pure CLI agent.

**But note only prompt-type objects are supported in the CLI.**

Other Drive object types (Workflow / Notebook) are unavailable in the CLI.
The official page states this explicitly.

Team sharing and Session Sharing are Business-and-above features.
sections.权限设计：三档值 + auto-approve:
It sets permissions per operation type independently:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `agent_decides` | proceeds on its own when confident, asks when unsure |
| `always_ask` | asks every time |
| `always_allow` | never asks |

**The default combination is the most worth recording.**
File edits default to `agent_decides`.
But the official docs say they **still prompt every time**, to guarantee reviewing the diff.

And auto-approve by default **bypasses the command denylist**.
Keeping the denylist requires turning that off manually.

But **denylists set by teams in the Admin Panel are never bypassed**.

"Individuals can bypass, admins cannot" — this asymmetry must be kept clear.
sections.核验说明:
Two reasons for `confidence: partial`.

- ✅ Verified: the five-tier structure and credit system, three entry points and the open-source client,
  local / cloud MCP support on both stacks, execution-profile three-tier values and auto-approve behavior,
  Warp Drive object types, tier caps on codebase indexing and cloud agents

- ❌ Not stated officially: context compaction strategy and cross-project memory boundaries, indexing algorithm and first-index time cost,
  Warp Factories' general availability timeline and final billing (see "Open questions")

**When citing this entry, use only the verified parts.**
